posts.author: Nick Timiraos
posts.text:
How would the Warsh Fed address market signals saying financial conditions are tightening, with an inflation picture that still looks uncomfortably hot? I wrote about the issue here: https://t.co/E5dwVHFA53  Despite some easy parallels to the December 2018 situation the Powell Fed faced (A new chair! Trump facing a midterm setback! A hawkish committee! Risk-off!), the inflation backdrop is so different that the comparison struggles to reveal much.

Consider: At that December meeting, the committee's leading intellectual dove, Jim Bullard of the St. Louis Fed, warned colleagues that raising rates risked looking "tone deaf." He presciently predicted that the yield curve would invert if they kept going. But he added a caveat that looks very different today: 

"Taking these types of risks at a meeting like this might be worth it if inflation was running above target and we really felt that we had to be aggressive to keep inflation and inflation expectations contained. But it's not running above target."

BREAKING: US new home sales jumped +14.2% MoM in October, to an annualized rate of 701,000 units, the highest since December 2025, crushing expectations of a -3.8% decline.

This marks the largest monthly increase since November 2025 and the 2nd-largest since August 2022.

It also marks a sharp recovery from the -9.7% MoM decline in September.

October's surge was driven by sales in the South, the nation's largest home-selling region, which soared +36.2% MoM, to an annualized rate of 515,000 units, the highest since March 2021.

At the same time, the median new home sale price fell -0.3% MoM and -3.2% YoY, to $391,300, the 2nd-lowest reading since July 2021.

Since the October 2022 peak, the median new home sale price has declined by $69,000, or -15.0%.

New home prices are falling sharply.

posts.text:
BREAKING: Two California companies are buying some of Nvidia’s most advanced chips, but both are actually Chinese-owned, per CBS

RiCloud AI (San Jose) is an Nvidia “preferred” cloud partner, which gives it priority access to advanced chips. Its parent is Yuxing InfoTech, based in Shenzhen and listed in Hong Kong. Its CEO, Cong Yu, holds a degree from a People’s Liberation Army military college. RiCloud got partner status about 10 weeks after it was incorporated.

Aivres is an Nvidia “elite” partner, the top tier. It was formerly called Inspur, after its Chinese parent, which the US blacklisted in 2023, and changed its name afterward. Citing an NYT analysis, CBS reports Aivres exported at least $5.6 billion in advanced technology to Southeast Asia, including about $3 billion in Blackwell-equipped computers. Some went to Megaspeed, the firm linked to Alice Huang, which provided AI cloud services to Alibaba and ByteDance.

The Fed is warning about “circular financing” in AI.

Big tech companies are lending to, investing in and guaranteeing smaller, riskier AI firms, which then buy their products, according to the Fed’s latest Financial Stability Report. In a downturn, the Fed says, their exposure “may be substantially larger than suggested by their on-balance-sheet liabilities.”

Nvidia alone has $530 billion in off-balance-sheet commitments, including up to $105 billion backing OpenAI’s Ohio data center.
